administrator_conclusions:
ESTABLISHED FINDINGS

“Pseudo-Bartter syndrome” should be presented as an acquired biochemical/physiological phenotype—typically hypokalaemic, hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis with chloride or volume depletion and secondary renin–angiotensin–aldosterone activation—not as proof of diuretic misuse, concealment, an eating disorder, or any particular intent. The phenotype can follow correctly prescribed treatment as well as non-prescribed exposure, vomiting, gastric drainage, chloride-losing diarrhoea, cystic-fibrosis sweat losses and other acquired renal salt-wasting states. Cause and intent require clinical history, medication reconciliation, repeated measurements and sometimes targeted testing.

DIFFERENTIAL AND TEST INTERPRETATION

• Active/recent loop or thiazide effect: urine chloride, sodium and potassium may be high because the drug is still producing renal salt delivery and distal potassium loss; values may fluctuate between samples. Renin and aldosterone are usually raised through volume contraction, blood pressure is often normal or low, magnesium may fall, and creatinine may rise with hypovolaemia. Prescribed exposure produces the same physiology as misuse.
• Remote exposure: after drug action has ended, urine chloride and drug testing may become negative or resemble an extrarenal chloride-depletion state, while alkalosis, potassium depletion or RAAS-driven sodium avidity may persist. A negative late screen therefore cannot exclude earlier use. No universal detection window was established: it depends on agent, dose, renal function, urine concentration, assay panel and analytical limit. The gathered evidence supports timing sensitivity but not a single public cutoff. A positive result establishes detected exposure, not dose, indication or intent.
• Vomiting, nasogastric drainage or pyloric obstruction: typically low urine chloride, often low urine sodium, hypokalaemia, high renin/aldosterone, normal/low blood pressure and possible prerenal azotaemia. Saline or other recent fluid treatment may raise urine electrolytes and invert the apparent pattern. Urine potassium is not cause-specific because aldosterone and distal sodium delivery affect it in several disorders.
• Bartter/Gitelman: usually persistently high urine chloride with renal Na/K loss, high renin/aldosterone and normal/low blood pressure. Gitelman more often has hypomagnesaemia and hypocalciuria; Bartter more often hypercalciuria/nephrocalcinosis. These are tendencies, not proofs: a 2022 single-centre whole-exome cohort of 63 patients (DOI 10.3390/ijms23105641; PMID 35628451; open full text) obtained a genetic diagnosis in 54/63, found substantial phenotype overlap and reported CKD in about 30%. The 2021 open-full-text CKJ review (DOI 10.1093/ckj/sfaa172; PMID 33564404) recommends serial rather than isolated urine chloride: intermittent diuretic effect may wax and wane, whereas inherited salt wasting is more persistently renal. Genetics may overturn apparently classic clinical clues.
• Mineralocorticoid states: hypertension shifts suspicion toward this branch but is not an absolute discriminator. Primary aldosteronism generally has suppressed renin with high aldosterone; Liddle syndrome or apparent mineralocorticoid excess generally suppress both. Urine chloride can remain high. Renin/aldosterone cannot be interpreted apart from volume/sodium status and relevant medications; the completed evidence did not support a DIY sampling or suppression-test algorithm.
• Cystic fibrosis/heavy sweat: open 2024 CF case literature documents extrarenal NaCl loss, low urine chloride, contraction and secondary hyperaldosteronism, sometimes presenting as pseudo-Bartter. Sweat chloride/CFTR assessment provides etiological evidence; the chemistry alone does not.
• Magnesium: low Mg supports, but does not uniquely identify, thiazide/loop exposure or Gitelman; diarrhoea and other medicines can also cause it. A 2026 full-text review cautions that serum Mg is an insensitive marker of total-body depletion.
• Other acquired mimics documented in the scientific review include colistin, aminoglycosides, amphotericin B, heavy metals, autoimmune tubulopathies and focal renal scarring with RAAS activation. Cystinosis, Dent disease and rarer transporter defects also enter specialist differentials.

LAXATIVES AND DIARRHOEA

“Laxatives cause pseudo-Bartter” is too broad. Ordinary bicarbonate-rich diarrhoeal loss usually causes normal-anion-gap metabolic acidosis, not alkalosis. Alkalosis can coexist with diarrhoea when chloride loss and volume contraction dominate—notably congenital chloride diarrhoea—or after complex chronic laxative exposure producing profound volume/chloride and potassium depletion. A 2024 case (DOI 10.1007/s13730-024-00851-9; PMID 38306007; case report, open PMC version retained) describes acquired pseudo-Bartter/Gitelman physiology with long-term laxative abuse and ESKD, but it cannot justify treating all diarrhoea or laxative use as pseudo-Bartter. The 2021 CKJ review cites stool chloride above 90 mEq/L as a clue in infant congenital chloride diarrhoea; cases from 2019 and 2025 show that urine or stool collected after infusions can be misleading. CF and congenital chloride diarrhoea can also coexist.

PHARMACOLOGY AND WITHDRAWAL CLAIMS

The audited drug claims were supported. The fully opened AEMPS furosemide SmPC (text revision May 2019) lists hypokalaemia, hypochloraemia, hypomagnesaemia, metabolic alkalosis and pseudo-Bartter with prolonged and/or improper use; DailyMed independently corroborates hypochloraemic alkalosis and K/Mg loss. A fully opened AEMPS hydrochlorothiazide-containing SmPC warns of hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia and hypochloraemic alkalosis. This establishes recognized adverse physiology, but the label’s reference to improper use must not be converted into an inference about an individual.

The opened AEMPS spironolactone SmPC confirms potentially severe hyperkalaemia, particularly with impaired kidney function, potassium supplements or other potassium-raising/RAAS-blocking drugs. Potassium-sparing agents are therefore not universally “safer” and no eating-disorder spironolactone regimen should be extrapolated to lipedema. The opened AEMPS acetazolamide SmPC confirms bicarbonate-loss physiology and risk of hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis; it can also cause electrolyte disturbances. A 2026 paediatric systematic review found only 11 studies and 736 children concerning acetazolamide and other rescue agents for hypochloraemic alkalosis, which is insufficient to support a public chronic-treatment protocol.

Rebound oedema after cessation is plausible and documented but heterogeneous. A 2016 eating-disorder review (DOI 10.1002/eat.22500; PMID 26875932; abstract opened) describes aldosterone-mediated salt/water retention after purging stops. A 1998 report of extreme diuretic dependence (DOI 10.1159/000013371; PMID 9730576; abstract opened) described severe withdrawal-related oedema, sometimes pulmonary oedema, with marked secondary hyperaldosteronism and sodium avidity. A fully inspected 1993 withdrawal thesis (DOI 10.26481/dis.19931201jj) adds adjacent evidence. These are not a universal timetable, tapering rule or indication for spironolactone; abrupt self-withdrawal and self-treatment should both be discouraged.

DIRECT LIPEDEMA EVIDENCE VERSUS EXTRAPOLATION

No direct lipedema–pseudo-Bartter cohort, case series or mechanism study was found. A targeted PubMed search returned zero records. The direct lipedema sources inspected—a 2011 single case (DOI 10.5535/arm.2011.35.6.922; PMID 22506222; full text) and a 2026 dermatology review (DOI 10.1016/j.abd.2025.501270; full text)—do not link lipedema itself to pseudo-Bartter. The 2026 review discourages long-term diuretics because they do not address the underlying lipedema process. Thus: absence of demonstrated lipedema causation is the direct finding; nephrology, pharmacology, CF and eating-disorder material is adjacent evidence; RAAS persistence is mechanistic inference supported by withdrawal reports; personal withdrawal stories remain anecdote.

DIAGNOSTIC TRAPS AND CONTRADICTIONS

Urine chloride is useful but not decisive. Active diuretics and inherited tubulopathies can both give high values; remote diuretics, vomiting and sweat/GI chloride loss can give low values; recent saline can alter the result. The 2012 AJKD case report (DOI 10.1053/j.ajkd.2011.11.033; PMID 22265393; abstract opened) emphasizes that history, volume status and urine chloride must be combined across vomiting, laxatives, mineralocorticoid agents, diuretics and alkali ingestion. A 1995 paediatric report (DOI 10.1007/BF00868731; PMID 8747119; abstract opened) found that blood and urine electrolytes alone could not distinguish furosemide ingestion from Bartter; urinary furosemide testing resolved that case. Conversely, absence from a late or incomplete screen does not exclude remote exposure. No robust source was completed for universal false-positive rates or one assay-independent detection window, so those should not be published.

SAFETY AND PUBLIC TRANSLATION

Urgent assessment is warranted for severe weakness or paralysis, palpitations/known arrhythmia or QT prolongation, syncope, confusion, respiratory compromise or marked breathlessness, oliguria/acute kidney injury, recurrent vomiting with weight loss, or infant failure to thrive. These abnormalities can cause dangerous arrhythmia and renal injury. Public wording should not recommend saline, potassium, magnesium, diuretic withdrawal, acetazolamide or spironolactone without individual medical assessment.

Suggested Spanish text: “El pseudo-Bartter describe un patrón adquirido de pérdida de cloro y potasio con alcalosis; no demuestra abuso, engaño ni una causa concreta. Puede aparecer durante o después de diuréticos prescritos, pero también con vómitos, drenaje gástrico, algunas pérdidas intestinales o de sudor y otros trastornos renales u hormonales. Un análisis aislado de orina o un cribado negativo no basta para saber la causa. Si tienes debilidad intensa, palpitaciones, desmayo, confusión, poca orina o falta de aire, busca atención médica urgente. Si tomas un diurético, no lo suspendas, reinicies ni sustituyas por espironolactona por tu cuenta; pide revisión médica y lleva la lista completa de medicamentos y suplementos.”

EVIDENCE QUALITY AND GAPS

Confidence is high for the pharmacology warnings and broad nephrology differential because official labels and multiple opened reviews agree. Confidence is moderate for rebound oedema because evidence is mainly reviews, a thesis and small/case-level reports. Direct lipedema causation is unsupported rather than disproven. The required Pro researcher was invoked twice, but both attempts failed before collecting evidence because ChatGPT browser navigation timed out; it contributed no substantive findings. Scientific and open-web researchers nevertheless completed extensive source-level review. A narrow CLI follow-up on laboratory assay specifications had not returned by synthesis, leaving precise screen-panel coverage, analytical interferences and numeric detection windows as explicit unresolved, laboratory-specific gaps.

researcher_responses.final_research_review:
I validated the Spanish lipedema page claims against current official labels and indexed medical literature. The strongest evidence came from AEMPS CIMA and DailyMed labels plus open-access PMC and PubMed records. Open/full-text status varied: the AEMPS and DailyMed drug labels were fully accessible as HTML/PDF-derived text; the PubMed items were abstract-only; the PMC items were open full text.

Core verification:
- Loop diuretic safety: the furosemide AEMPS SmPC explicitly lists hypopotasemia, hipocloremia, hipomagnesemia and alcalosis metabólica, and it even names síndrome de pseudo Bartter in misuse and/or prolonged use. The DailyMed furosemide label independently confirms hypokalemia and hypochloremic alkalosis, and it lists hypomagnesemia among expected electrolyte losses. Mechanistically, the DailyMed label also states that furosemide blocks Na-K-2Cl in the loop of Henle and increases potassium and magnesium excretion. This is strong label-level support.
- Thiazide safety: the AEMPS hydrochlorothiazide-containing label states that thiazides can precipitate new hypokalaemia, worsen pre-existing hypokalaemia, and trigger hypomagnesaemia. It also says thiazides can precipitate a hypochloraemic alkalosis. The label further notes arrhythmia risk when thiazide-induced hypokalaemia/hypomagnesaemia is present. This is also strong label-level support.
- Potassium-sparing drugs: the AEMPS spironolactone label explicitly warns that spironolactone can produce hyperkalaemia, that the risk rises with reduced renal function, and that concomitant potassium supplements or other potassium-sparing / RAAS-blocking drugs can cause severe hyperkalaemia. So spironolactone is not a low-risk option in the way some lay pages imply.
- Acetazolamide: the AEMPS acetazolamide label explicitly warns about metabolic acidosis and states that the drug can cause electrolyte changes including transient hypokalaemia and acidosis. The label also describes hyperchloraemic acidosis as a relevant condition/caution, which fits bicarbonate loss physiology.

Pseudo-Bartter is better treated as acquired physiology, not as an intent diagnosis.
- The 2016 eating-disorder review (PMID 26875932, DOI 10.1002/eat.22500) states that pseudo-Bartter syndrome is the root cause of many complications when purging stops and that aldosterone-driven salt/water retention can produce severe edema. This is a physiologic state after chloride depletion and RAAS activation; it is not proof of deception or abuse.
- The 2012 nephrology case report (PMID 22265393, DOI 10.1053/j.ajkd.2011.11.033) says the history plus volume status plus urine chloride help, but that surreptitious vomiting, mineralocorticoid-active agents, laxatives, diuretics, and alkali ingestion can all create similar pictures. It is an important trap: urine chloride is useful, but not definitive for intent.
- The 1995 pediatric report (PMID 8747119, DOI 10.1007/BF00868731) is a classic warning that blood and urinary electrolytes alone cannot distinguish diuretic ingestion from true Bartter syndrome; the urine contained frusemide, and a diuretic screen was warranted. This supports the distinction between phenotype and cause.
- The 2024 laxative-abuse case (PMID 38306007, DOI 10.1007/s13730-024-00851-9) explicitly defines pseudo-Bartter/Gitelman syndrome as a disorder with hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis due to secondary factors such as lifestyle and/or medicines. That supports descriptive acquired physiology, not moral judgment.

Rebound edema after stopping chronic diuretics: evidence exists, but it is limited and not protocolizable.
- The 1998 case report on extreme diuretic dependence (PMID 9730576, DOI 10.1159/000013371) describes withdrawal causing severe cardiorespiratory failure, sometimes pulmonary edema, in diuretic-dependent idiopathic edema, with extreme secondary hyperaldosteronism and persistent tubular sodium avidity. This supports a rebound edema mechanism in selected patients.
- However, the evidence base here is case-report level plus qualitative review, not a universal timeline or withdrawal algorithm. It is not safe to imply a single time course, or to give a one-size-fits-all taper and rescue protocol, especially for a public patient page.

Urine chloride and diuretic-screen caveats:
- The 2025 acid-base review (PMID 39964926; abstract-only) states that evaluation of metabolic alkalosis begins with urine chloride to determine whether the process is chloride depletion. That is a good first step, but only a first step.
- The furosemide label and case literature together support a timing caveat: furosemide has a short oral onset, a 6-8 hour diuretic effect, and an approximately 2 hour terminal half-life, so remote exposure may no longer be detectable when the patient is tested. A negative screen therefore does not exclude earlier exposure.
- Differential traps that remain legitimate include vomiting or gastric drainage, laxative/diarrhea-related chloride loss, mineralocorticoid excess, Bartter/Gitelman syndromes, CF with heavy sweat salt loss, and diuretic misuse. The phenotype alone does not establish intent.

CF/heavy-sweat evidence:
- The open-access CF case/review in PMC states that excessive sweat sodium chloride losses from dysfunctional CFTR cause volume contraction and secondary hyperaldosteronism, leading to renal potassium loss and metabolic alkalosis. It also documents low urine chloride and positive sweat chloride testing.
- The 2024 three-case CF review (open access in PMC) again frames hypokalemic hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis as pseudo-Bartter syndrome due to CF-related salt loss. This is useful adjacent evidence for the mechanism, even though it is not lipedema-specific.

Direct lipedema evidence:
- In this run, a targeted PubMed search for lipedema + pseudo-Bartter returned no records. I did not find direct lipedema-specific evidence that the lipedema condition itself causes pseudo-Bartter or that there is a lipedema-specific diuretic safety protocol addressing this phenotype. That absence should be stated plainly on the page.

Practical Spanish wording that stays safe:
La pseudo-Bartter es un patrón fisiológico adquirido, no una prueba de abuso ni de intención. Puede aparecer con diuréticos, vómitos, laxantes, pérdidas intensas de sal/sudor, fármacos con efecto mineralocorticoide o trastornos renales como Bartter/Gitelman. En lipedema no hay evidencia directa suficiente para atribuir este cuadro al propio lipedema. Si aparecen debilidad marcada, palpitaciones, desmayo, calambres intensos, confusión o falta de aire, hay que buscar atención médica. No suspendas ni ajustes diuréticos por tu cuenta, y no uses espironolactona sin supervisión porque puede causar hiperpotasemia.

Overall conclusion: the Spanish page can safely state that loop/thiazide labels support hypokalaemia, hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis and magnesium loss; spironolactone can cause hyperkalaemia; acetazolamide tends toward bicarbonate loss/metabolic acidosis; pseudo-Bartter is a descriptive acquired physiology; rebound edema after diuretic withdrawal is real but not universal; and there is no direct lipedema-specific evidence strong enough to justify a lipedema-native pseudo-Bartter claim or a fixed withdrawal protocol.

researcher_responses.final_research_review:
Bottom line: pseudo-Bartter is best treated as an acquired hypokalaemic, hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis phenotype, not a single disease. Across the full-text sources I inspected, the key discriminator is whether the alkalosis is chloride-responsive and whether chloride loss is renal or extrarenal. Low urine chloride supports vomiting, nasogastric drainage, pyloric obstruction, congenital chloride diarrhea, or CF-related salt loss; persistently high urine chloride with high renin/aldosterone and normal or low BP supports Bartter/Gitelman or active diuretic effect; hypertension shifts the differential toward mineralocorticoid excess. A single spot urine can mislead after saline, after recent drug withdrawal, or when samples are collected at the wrong time.

Representative open full-text sources: the 2021 Clinical Kidney Journal review on Bartter/Gitelman/pseudo-Bartter (DOI 10.1093/ckj/sfaa172, PMID 33564404; narrative review) states that repeated urine chloride helps identify diuretic abuse because values wax and wane day to day, whereas Bartter keeps urine chloride persistently elevated; it also gives the practical clue that fecal chloride >90 mEq/L is diagnostic in infant congenital chloride diarrhea. The 2018 Bartter review (DOI 10.2147/IJNRD.S155397; narrative review) adds that a thiazide challenge requires a 7-day washout, K and Mg supplements only, and is not routinely recommended because of volume depletion risk. The 2022 cohort of 63 Bartter/Gitelman patients (DOI 10.3390/ijms23105641, PMID 35628451; single-institution WES cohort) found 54/63 diagnostic yield, substantial phenotype overlap, and CKD in about 30%, so age at onset, prematurity, nephrocalcinosis, and even BP are helpful but not absolute.

Differential and expected patterns:
- Active/recent loop or thiazide exposure: urine Cl/Na/K often high and variable; Mg often low; renin and aldosterone high; BP usually normal/low; creatinine can rise if volume depleted. Direct diuretic assays are time-sensitive: the classic 1981 furosemide-abuse case (DOI 10.2169/internalmedicine1962.20.216; case report + literature review) confirmed furosemide in plasma and urine by HPLC despite denial.
- Remote exposure / after withdrawal: biochemical abnormalities may partially normalize or become misleading, but physiology can linger. The 1993 diuretic-withdrawal thesis (DOI 10.26481/dis.19931201jj; withdrawal trial review) describes rebound edema and weight gain after stopping chronic diuretics and links chronic use to secondary hyperaldosteronism and metabolic alkalosis.
- Vomiting or gastric drainage: low urine Cl is expected; urine Na often low; K low/variable; renin and aldosterone high from volume contraction; BP low/normal; Mg may be low-normal; prerenal azotaemia may appear. Urine Cl drawn after saline can rise and mislead.
- Congenital chloride diarrhea and CF sweat-salt loss: extrarenal chloride loss gives low urine Cl/Na; stool chloride is high in CCD; sweat chloride and CFTR testing help in CF; dehydration can raise creatinine. The 2019 Brazilian CCD misdiagnosis case and the 2025 infant diarrhea case both show sample-timing traps: stool or urine drawn after infusion can invert the apparent picture.
- Bartter/Gitelman: urine Cl is persistently high; urine Na/K usually high; renin and aldosterone high; BP normal/low. GS typically has hypomagnesaemia and hypocalciuria; BS more often has hypercalciuria/nephrocalcinosis, but overlap is common. The 2021 Bartter/Gitelman primer and the 2022 cohort both stress that genotype can overturn apparently classic clinical clues.
- Mineralocorticoid excess: hypertension is the branch point. Primary aldosteronism has low renin/high aldosterone; Liddle or apparent mineralocorticoid excess have low renin/low aldosterone. Urine Cl may be high because the kidney is still wasting sodium and potassium.
- Laxatives and diarrhea: the blanket claim that laxatives cause pseudo-Bartter is overbroad. Ordinary diarrhoea usually causes normal-anion-gap metabolic acidosis, not alkalosis. The true alkalotic diarrhea edge cases I found are chloride-losing diarrheas, especially congenital chloride diarrhea and some CF-related states. Chronic laxative abuse can still produce PBS/PGS when the net effect is volume and chloride depletion; a 2024 case report shows progression to ESKD.
- Additional mimics: colistin, aminoglycosides, amphotericin B, heavy metals, autoimmune tubulopathies, cystinosis, Dent disease, claudin-10b defects, Kir4.1 defects, and focal renal scarring with RAAS activation.

Pharmacology audit: loop and thiazide diuretics are the archetypal cause of the phenotype; K-sparing agents such as amiloride, triamterene, spironolactone, and eplerenone are corrective adjuncts in proven renal salt wasting or mineralocorticoid states, not lipedema-specific therapy. Acetazolamide does induce bicarbonaturia/metabolic acidosis and can be used as rescue therapy in hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis, but evidence is limited. The 2026 systematic review of pediatric hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis found only 11 studies and 736 children, with acetazolamide, arginine chloride, hydrochloric acid, and ammonium chloride reported, so this is a rescue-space evidence base, not a routine chronic strategy. Rebound edema after stopping chronic diuretics is biologically plausible and documented, but that does not justify importing an eating-disorder spironolactone protocol into lipedema. The 2026 lipedema review explicitly discourages long-term diuretics because they do not address the underlying lipedema process.

Direct lipedema evidence: I found direct lipedema literature, but no direct lipedema pseudo-Bartter cohort, case series, or mechanistic paper. The only lipedema sources retained were a 2011 case report (DOI 10.5535/arm.2011.35.6.922, PMID 22506222; single case) and a 2026 dermatology review (DOI 10.1016/j.abd.2025.501270; review). Neither links lipedema itself to pseudo-Bartter or acquired alkalosis. Searches for lipedema + pseudo-Bartter, lipedema + diuretics, and lipedema + spironolactone returned adjacent management literature only, not direct evidence. For a Spanish patient-facing lipedema site, it is therefore safer to say that lipedema is not established as a pseudo-Bartter state.

Conservative red flags: severe weakness or paralysis, arrhythmia or QT prolongation, respiratory compromise, syncope, oliguria or AKI, recurrent vomiting with weight loss, infant failure to thrive, and persistent alkalosis despite denial of diuretics. Those patterns warrant urgent evaluation with careful volume/chloride repletion, repeat urine chloride, Mg assessment, and exposure review rather than reflex chronic diuretic use. All relied-on evidence was inspected as full text or extracted text; no search snippet was used as proof.

key_artifacts.description: StatPearls hypokalemia text used for urine potassium thresholds, chloride-responsive vs resistant alkalosis, BP-linked branching, and the core vomiting/diuretic/mineralocorticoid differential.
StatPearls diuretics chapter used for loop and thiazide pharmacology, K-sparing agents, RAAS effects, and acetazolamide’s metabolic-acidosis mechanism.

1981 pseudo-Bartter due to furosemide abuse case plus Japanese literature review. Used for active nonprescribed loop exposure, HPLC confirmation in plasma and urine, and reversibility after stopping furosemide.
2011 lipedema case report. Direct lipedema evidence only; used to confirm lipedema literature exists but does not support a pseudo-Bartter linkage or routine diuretic treatment.
2019 congenital chloride diarrhea misdiagnosed as Bartter. Used for sample-timing pitfalls, low fecal chloride during dehydration, and misleading urine and fecal chloride after infusion.
1993 diuretic-withdrawal thesis used for rebound edema and weight gain after stopping chronic diuretics and for RAAS/secondary hyperaldosteronism physiology in prescribed edema treatment.
2025 infant hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis with diarrhea. Used to show low urine chloride in a chloride-losing diarrhoea edge case and the role of fecal chloride plus genetics.
2024 BMJ case report of pseudo-Bartter as the initial presentation of CF. Used for sweat-salt loss phenotype, low urine electrolytes, and CF consideration in infants with alkalosis.
2024 case report of pseudo-Bartter/Gitelman from long-term laxative abuse causing ESKD. Used to support chronic laxative abuse as a PBS/PGS cause with renal consequences.
2024 acquired Bartter-like syndrome from colistin. Used as a drug-induced mimic with hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, hypomagnesemia, and rapid improvement after stopping colistin.
2025 CF-related kidney disease review. Used for the standard pseudo-Bartter workup in CF: serum electrolytes, venous blood gas, urine electrolytes, sweat chloride, and broader kidney complications.
2025 case report on prolonged hypokalemia after trigger removal in pseudo-Bartter/Gitelman. Used to show biochemical abnormalities can persist long after the apparent cause is removed.
2026 lipedema dermatology review. Used for direct lipedema evidence and the statement that long-term diuretics are discouraged because they do not address the underlying lipedema process.
2026 systematic review of pediatric hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis therapy. Used to audit acetazolamide, hydrochloric acid, ammonium chloride, and arginine chloride as limited rescue options.
2026 hypomagnesemia review. Used for diuretics, chronic diarrhea, and medication causes of magnesium deficiency, plus the point that serum Mg is an insensitive total-body marker.
2026 pseudo-Bartter case from focal renal scarring. Used for RAAS-driven pseudo-Bartter without diuretics, and for the urine electrolyte response before and after saline infusion.
2009 autopsy report on pseudo-Bartter from diuretics and diet pills. Used for nonprescribed exposure, severe alkalosis, renal calcification, and toxicology/autopsy confirmation of furosemide.
2011 lipedema case report. Adjacent lipedema evidence only; helps distinguish lipedema management literature from pseudo-Bartter literature and shows no direct diuretic mechanism claim.
2017 review of normal anion gap metabolic acidosis. Used to contrast ordinary diarrhoea with acidosis and support that alkalotic diarrhoea is atypical and should trigger chloride-loss thinking.

2018 Bartter causes-diagnosis-treatment review. Used for urine chloride in vomiting/bulimia, serial urine chloride for diuretic abuse, and the 7-day thiazide washout test with its volume-depletion caveat.
2020 CF plus congenital chloride diarrhea case. Used to show that CF and CCD can coexist, pseudo-Bartter may persist despite salt therapy, and stool electrolytes plus genetics may be needed.

2021 CKJ differential review of Bartter, Gitelman, and pseudo-Bartter. Used for the urine chloride table, the CF/CCD/vomiting/diuretic-abuse distinctions, and day-to-day variability in diuretic misuse.
2021 Bartter/Gitelman primer. Used for the core phenotype, hypocalciuria, hypomagnesemia, hyperreninemia, secondary hyperaldosteronism, and the hypertension contrast with mineralocorticoid excess.
2022 63-patient Bartter/Gitelman cohort with WES. Used to quantify overlap, show 54/63 diagnostic yield, and document CKD in about 30% of patients despite variable clinical clues.
